519.title: The poets
519.hook: the surah's name, and the poets excepted who believe, do good and remember Allah (26:224–227)
519.howItsDone: Muslims across the world sing and recite devotional poetry, from Arabic odes praising the Prophet to nasheeds and qawwali, while scholars hold that the Qur'an itself is not poetry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, khafd al-janah, and your line was lower the wing. Did you listen all the way to the end before answering? Day five hundred nineteen.

In the Arabia the Prophet grew up in, the old histories describe the poet as no quiet figure with a notebook. A poet could be a weapon and a newspaper at once. A tribe's poet praised his own people and mocked their rivals, and a sharp line in verse could travel from camp to camp and stick to a family's name. So when the Prophet began reciting the Qur'an, some of his opponents had a label ready. He's just a poet. Surah Ash-Shu'ara, named for the poets, ends by answering that.

The last verses of the surah describe the poets of that time without much sympathy. Those who go astray follow them. They wander in every valley, as the image goes, chasing any mood or theme, and they say what they don't do. Commentators read this as the answer to the label: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, they say, was not wandering, and did what he said. The Qur'an says plainly elsewhere that it is not the word of a poet. But then comes a turn, an exception, in the very last verse. Except those who believe, and do good works, and remember God much, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. So the surah doesn't ban poetry. It sorts it. Words that wander, and words that remember. The exception had faces. The Prophet had poets among his companions, Hassan ibn Thabit among them. A report in Bukhari says the Prophet asked Hassan to answer the Quraysh's satires in verse, and prayed that God support him with the Holy Spirit, which Muslims understand as the angel Jibril. Another hadith in Bukhari says that some poetry is wisdom. Later, a poet named Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, who had written against the Prophet, came to him and recited a famous ode, and tradition says the Prophet gave him his own cloak. Scholars discuss the strength of that story's chains. From those beginnings grew a long tradition of praise poems for the Prophet, in Arabic and in many other languages, sung at weddings and gatherings. The test the surah gives is simple. Do the words remember God, and do the people saying them live them?

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one devotional poem. Sit, and let the breath settle. If you know one by heart, a line of a nasheed, a verse someone once sang to you, a praise poem from your own language, let it play slowly in your mind. If you don't, decide which one you'll look up today: an Arabic ode, a Persian or Urdu poem, anything written to remember God. Notice what the words do to your breathing. Notice which line you'd want to keep. If you pray, you can say that line as a prayer. The bell holds the time.
The poets. Ash-Shu'ara, the surah named for them, which turns away the poets who wander and keeps the ones who believe, do good and remember God much. Today's word.
Your line: words that remember. Today, send one line of good poetry, or one line of praise, to someone who could use it. Day five hundred nineteen.

520.title: The ant's warning
520.hook: an ant warns the others to hide from Sulayman's army, and he smiles and prays in thanks (27:18–19)
520.howItsDone: Muslims recite Sulayman's prayer of thanks from 27:19, and many cite the Prophet's prohibition on killing ants and bees as part of Islamic care for animals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poets, and your line was words that remember. Whose day did your line of poetry land in? Day five hundred twenty, and a new surah.

People, jinn and birds, all marching in ranks. That's Sulayman's army in Surah An-Naml, the Ant, the twenty-seventh: hosts gathered for him and set in order, moving across the land. And somewhere at ankle height, in a valley, one tiny creature sees it coming. It doesn't run for itself. It turns around and calls to everyone else, before it is too late. The surah is named for that moment, and for that one small voice.
screen: `AN ARMY OF PEOPLE, JINN AND BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Sulayman, the surah says, had been taught the speech of birds. So when the army reaches the Valley of the Ants, he hears this. Pickthall: "O ants! Enter your dwellings lest Solomon and his armies crush you, unperceiving." Notice that last word. The ant doesn't call the army cruel. She says they'll crush us without noticing. She gives a great king the benefit of the doubt, even while she gets everyone out of the way. In Arabic, the ant is feminine, a namla, and the verbs follow. And then the king's reaction. Pickthall: "And (Solomon) smiled, laughing at her speech". No anger, no order to halt and punish. And straight away he turns it into a prayer: my Lord, make me thankful for Your favor on me and my parents, and to do good that pleases Thee. A king hears an insect's voice, and his first words are thanks. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ took the small creatures seriously too. A hadith in Bukhari tells of an earlier prophet, stung by an ant, who had the whole colony burned, and God rebuked him: because one ant stung you, you burned a whole nation that glorified Me? And in Abu Dawud, the Prophet forbade killing four creatures, and the ant is first on the list. The bee, the hoopoe and a small bird of prey are the others. So the story turns the usual picture upside down. The power is all on one side, and the attention, the smile and the thanks go the other way.
screen: `SULAYMAN KNEW THE SPEECH OF BIRDS.` · `CRUSH YOU, UNPERCEIVING.` · `HE SMILED, AND GAVE THANKS.` · `A NATION THAT GLORIFIED ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: step around an ant. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of the smallest living things you share space with: ants on the pavement, a spider in the corner, the birds you never look at. Picture walking out of your door today and seeing a line of ants crossing the path. Picture stopping, watching them for a moment, and stepping around. Notice what it feels like to make yourself slightly less convenient for something tiny. If you pray, you can say Sulayman's words of thanks. The bell holds the time.

Your line: he smiled at the ant. Today, when something small gets in your way, smile at it instead of brushing it aside. Day five hundred twenty.

521.title: The hoopoe's news
521.hook: a small bird brings Sulayman news of a queen who worships the sun (27:20–26)
521.howItsDone: Muslims read the hoopoe's story in Surah An-Naml as a lesson in listening carefully and verifying news, and the hoopoe is among the creatures a hadith says not to kill.

segments.voice: Yesterday, namla, and your line was he smiled at the ant. What small thing got in your way, and did you smile at it? Day five hundred twenty-one.

Sulayman is inspecting the birds, one by one, the way a commander walks down a line of troops. And there's a gap. He says, why don't I see the hoopoe? Is it absent? The hoopoe is a striking little bird, cinnamon-colored, with a crest that fans open like a crown and wings barred black and white. Sulayman is not pleased. He says he'll punish it severely, unless it brings him a clear excuse. And then, not long after, the hoopoe lands.

What the hoopoe says first is astonishing, given who it's talking to. In the Arabic, it tells the king: I have encompassed what you have not encompassed. Pickthall renders the next words: "I come unto thee from Sheba with sure tidings." A bird the size of your hand tells the man who speaks to birds and commands jinn that it knows something he doesn't. And then it reports, carefully, like a good scout. There's a woman ruling the people of Saba', Sheba. She's been given something of everything, and she has a great throne. And the hoopoe saw her and her people bowing to the sun instead of God, because Shaytan had made their deeds look fair to them. The hoopoe even adds a short reflection of its own, about God who brings out what is hidden in the heavens and the earth. Then look at how Sulayman responds. He doesn't wave the bird away because it's small, or punish it for speaking boldly. He doesn't simply believe it either. He says: we shall see whether you have told the truth or are one of the liars. And he sends the hoopoe back with a letter. That's the shape of the whole scene: listen to the small voice, then check it. Some commentators tell a story that the hoopoe could sense water under the ground, and that Sulayman's army relied on it. That's a story people tell, from later commentary, not from the verse. The verse gives us enough. A king who did a roll call and noticed one bird was missing, and a bird who came back knowing something he didn't.
screen: `I KNOW WHAT YOU DON'T.` · `SURE TIDINGS FROM SHEBA.` · `A QUEEN, A THRONE, THE SUN.` · `WE SHALL SEE IF YOU SPEAK TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to someone small. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone whose voice usually gets passed over. A child at the table. The newest person at work. The quiet one in the group chat. The person who cleans the building. What might they know that you don't? Picture asking them a real question today and actually waiting for the answer. Picture taking it seriously enough to check it, the way Sulayman did. If you pray, you can ask for the humility to be told something new. The bell holds the time.
Hoopoe. The small bird who came back to Sulayman knowing something he didn't, sure tidings from Sheba.
Your line: the hoopoe knew. Today, ask the quietest person you meet one real question, and listen all the way through. Day five hundred twenty-one.

522.title: The Queen of Sheba
522.hook: Bilqis consults her council, tests Sulayman, and submits with him to the Lord of the worlds (27:29–44)
522.howItsDone: Muslims often cite the Queen of Sheba's council as an example of shura, consultation, and many pray istikhara, the prayer for guidance, before a big decision.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hoopoe's news, and your line was the hoopoe knew. Who did you ask a real question, and what did they know? Day five hundred twenty-two.

A letter lands in a throne room in Sheba. Sulayman has sent the hoopoe with it and told the bird to throw it down to them. The queen opens it in front of her nobles. It's from a foreign king, and it's short: it opens in the name of God, the Merciful, and tells her not to rise up in pride against him but to come to him in surrender. A letter like that could start a war by evening. Watch what this queen does instead.

First, she reads it aloud and tells her council it's a noble letter, and she quotes its opening. Pickthall: "Lo! it is from Solomon, and lo! it is: In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful". That's the bismillah, appearing inside a surah's verse, in a queen's mouth. Then she consults. She tells her chiefs she decides nothing until they are present. They answer like soldiers: we have strength and great might, but the command is yours. And she doesn't reach for the might. She says kings, when they enter a town, ruin it and make its honored people humble. That is her reason for caution. So she tests him instead. She sends a gift, and waits to see what comes back. Sulayman refuses it: what God has given me, he says, is better than what He has given you. Then she travels to him. Her throne has been brought there before her, disguised, and she's asked, is your throne like this? Her answer is careful: it's as though it were the very one. Then she's led into a hall, and thinking the floor is a pool of water, she lifts her skirt. It's smooth glass. And at that moment she speaks the surah's climax. Pickthall: "I surrender with Solomon unto Allah, the Lord of the Worlds." With Solomon, not to him. The Qur'an never gives her name. Muslim tradition calls her Bilqis; the Hebrew Bible also tells of a Queen of Sheba who visited Solomon with hard questions. But in An-Naml, what stands out is her method. She consulted, avoided war, tested, looked closely, and when she saw, she said so.
screen: `A NOBLE LETTER: IN THE NAME OF GOD.` · `I DECIDE NOTHING WITHOUT YOU.` · `A GIFT, A THRONE, A FLOOR OF GLASS.` · `WITH SOLOMON, TO THE LORD OF THE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: consult before a big decision. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one decision that's coming up. A move, a job, a hard conversation, a purchase you're not sure of. Notice whether you've already decided alone, quickly. Now think of two or three people whose judgment you trust. What would you ask them? Picture yourself, like the queen, laying it out plainly and actually listening. If you pray, you can make istikhara, the prayer for guidance, or simply ask for a clear head. The bell holds the time.
Bilqis. Muslim tradition's name for the Queen of Sheba in An-Naml, who consulted her council, tested Sulayman, looked closely, and surrendered with him to the Lord of the worlds. Today's word.
Your line: she thought it through. Today, before you decide the decision you just pictured, ask one person you trust what they think. Day five hundred twenty-two.

523.title: Who answers the distressed
523.hook: who answers the one in distress when he calls, and removes the evil (27:62)
523.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite 27:62 in times of trouble and call on God in their own words in du'a, believing that the prayer of the one in distress is heard.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bilqis, and your line was she thought it through. Who did you ask before deciding, and what did they say? Day five hundred twenty-three.

The car skids on ice. The doctor walks in with a face that's too careful. In that second, before any thinking, some people who rarely pray hear themselves say something like please, God. Not a formal prayer. Just a call, with nothing else left to try. Near the end of An-Naml, the surah lists the signs of God in a run of questions, and one of them is exactly about that moment.

The passage goes like a drumbeat. Who created the heavens and the earth and sent down rain, and grew gardens with it? Is there a god beside God? Who made the earth a fixed place, and ran rivers through it, and set the mountains, and put a barrier between the two seas? Is there a god beside God? And then the third question, verse sixty-two. Who answers the one in distress when he calls on Him, and removes the evil, and makes you successors on the earth? Is there a god beside God? The word for the distressed is al-mudtarr. The classical dictionaries give it the sense of being forced, compelled, driven into a corner. Not just sad. Someone with no other options left. And the verse doesn't say who answers the righteous, or the one who prays perfectly. It says the cornered one, when he calls. Commentators noticed this, and some link it to another passage where people in a storm at sea call on God sincerely, and then, safe on land, forget. The call itself is heard. That's why the verse sits among the signs, with rain and rivers and mountains. Being answered in a corner is presented as something people know from their own lives, a piece of evidence as plain as weather. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi names three prayers that are answered without doubt: the prayer of the one who is wronged, of the traveler, and of a parent. Muslim teachers add that being answered doesn't always mean getting exactly what was asked. In their reading, what the verse promises is that the call is heard.
screen: `IS THERE A GOD BESIDE GOD?` · `RAIN, RIVERS, MOUNTAINS, SEAS.` · `AL-MUDTARR: THE CORNERED ONE.` · `THE CALL IS HEARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: call on Him in one worry. Sit, and let the breath settle. Find the worry you've been carrying around this week, the one that sits under everything. Don't try to solve it. Just name it, plainly, in your own words. Notice where it sits in your body. If you pray, you can call on God with it now, in whatever language comes, the way the verse describes. If you don't, you can simply say it out loud to the quiet, and set it down for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Al-mudtarr. The cornered, distressed one, named in An-Naml's question of who answers them when they call and lifts the harm. Today's word.
Your line: he answers the distressed. Today, check in on one person you know is in a corner right now, and just ask how they are. Day five hundred twenty-three.

524.title: A mother's empty heart
524.hook: Musa's mother's heart became empty, and Allah steadied it (28:10)
524.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Musa's mother in Al-Qasas as a picture of trust in God under fear, and many recite its promise, We will bring him back to you, in times of separation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-mudtarr, and your line was he answers the distressed. Who did you check in on, and how were they? Day five hundred twenty-four, and a new surah.

Surah Al-Qasas, the Stories, the twenty-eighth, tells Musa's life from the very beginning. And it begins not with Musa but with his mother. Pharaoh is killing the newborn boys of the Children of Israel. She has just had a son. And she is told, by an inspiration from God, to nurse him, and when she fears for him, to put him in a chest, as another surah tells it, and cast him into the river. Don't fear, don't grieve, the verse says: We will bring him back to you. So she does it. She sets her baby on moving water and lets go. Then comes the next morning.

The Qur'an doesn't skip over what she felt. Pickthall: "And the heart of the mother of Moses became void". Empty. The Arabic is farigh, emptied out, vacant. Commentators asked: empty of what? Some said empty of everything except Musa; she couldn't think of anything else. Others said empty of patience, or of the calm she'd had the night before. The verse goes on: she was about to give him away, to blurt out that the child was hers, had God not strengthened her heart. The word there is rabatna, We tied, We bound: the verb for tying something fast so it doesn't drift. And the verse says why: so that she would be among the believers, those who trust. Notice what God doesn't do. He doesn't take the fear away. Her heart is still empty. He ties it down so that it holds. Then she does something very practical. She tells Musa's sister, follow him. The girl watches from a distance as the child reaches Pharaoh's household. God had kept him from taking any wet nurse. And the sister steps forward and says, shall I show you a family who will look after him? So Musa comes home, fed at his own mother's breast, inside Pharaoh's household. The verse says it was so that her eye would be cooled and she wouldn't grieve, and so she would know God's promise is true. The empty heart stays in the story. In this telling, faith isn't the absence of panic. It's a heart held steady while it's still afraid.
screen: `HER HEART BECAME EMPTY.` · `RABATNA: WE TIED IT DOWN.` · `THE SISTER FOLLOWS FROM AFAR.` · `HOME TO HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: steady someone who is afraid. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone you know who is waiting for something frightening right now. Results, a court date, a child far from home, a hospital bed. Picture their face. Notice what they might need: not advice, not cheerfulness, just someone to sit with them so their heart doesn't drift. Decide what you can offer this week, a call, a visit, a meal, a message that says I'm here. If you pray, you can ask that their heart be tied steady. The bell holds the time.
Farigh. Empty, vacant: how Musa's mother's heart was left after the river, emptied of everything but her son, and held steady by God until he came home. Today's word.
Your line: a heart held steady. Today, send the message to the person you thought of. Keep it short, and don't try to fix anything. Day five hundred twenty-four.

525.title: Walking with modesty
525.hook: one of the two women comes to him walking with modesty (28:25)
525.howItsDone: Muslims speak of haya' as a quality of character for both men and women, shown in speech, bearing and conduct, and many recite Musa's prayer from 28:24 in times of need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, farigh, and your line was a heart held steady. Did you send the short message to someone who's afraid? Day five hundred twenty-five, the end of the week.

Musa is a grown man now, and on the run. He has fled Egypt, alone, and walked all the way to Madyan. He arrives at a well where shepherds are crowding their flocks in to drink. Standing back, holding their animals away, are two women. He asks what's wrong. They say they can't water until the shepherds leave, and their father is a very old man. So Musa waters their flock for them. Then he goes and sits in the shade, exhausted, with nothing, and prays. And then someone comes walking toward him.
screen: `A MAN ON THE RUN, AT A WELL.`
`HE SITS IN THE SHADE AND PRAYS.`

segments.voice: His prayer in the shade is one line long. Pickthall: "My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me." No plan, no demand. Just: I need whatever You send. And what's sent comes walking. Pickthall: "Then there came unto him one of the two women, walking shyly." The Arabic says she walked 'ala istihya', upon shyness, upon modesty. The classical dictionaries put that word under the same root as haya', today's word, and as hayat, life. Some classical scholars, Ibn al-Qayyim among them, drew the connection: haya' keeps a heart alive. Then there's a detail in the verse itself. The Qur'an describes her modesty by the way she walks. Not her clothes; the verse doesn't mention them. Her pace, her bearing. And in the same verse she speaks, clearly and directly, to a stranger: my father invites you, to pay you for watering for us. Modesty here isn't silence or shrinking. It's a way of carrying yourself that's dignified and unhurried, while still saying exactly what needs saying. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says haya' is a branch of faith. Another, in Bukhari, says haya' brings nothing but good. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself was described by a companion as shyer than a young woman behind her curtain, so haya' in Islam was never only for women. This week has been full of people who carry themselves well. The poets who remember. A king who smiled at an ant. A bird who knew. A queen who thought it through. Al-mudtarr. A heart held steady. And today, a woman whose modesty is a walk.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry yourself gently. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice your posture right now. Shoulders, jaw, hands. Then picture walking into the next room you'll enter today, a kitchen, an office, a classroom. Picture walking in without rushing, without performing, without shrinking either. Just at an even pace, with your head level. Picture saying what you need to say simply, and stopping. If you pray, you can repeat Musa's words from the shade: my Lord, I need whatever good You send me. The bell holds the time.
Haya'. Modesty, shyness, a sense of dignity before God and people; in the hadith, a branch of faith that brings nothing but good. Today's word.
Your line: modesty is a walk. Today, walk into one room more slowly than usual, and say one thing plainly. Day five hundred twenty-five.
